analysis.one_liner: Phases the capital gains tax rate down to zero and lets investors adjust gains for inflation.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have cut the capital gains rate from 20% in 1997 to 0% by 2017, died in the Ways and Means Committee with no cosponsors and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have cut the tax rate on investment gains from 20% in 1997 down one percentage point a year to zero by 2017. It also would have let investors raise the "purchase price" of stocks, real estate, and other assets held more than three years to reflect inflation, shrinking the gain that gets taxed. The bill never left the House Ways and Means Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: People who sell stocks, business interests, and other capital assets would pay steadily less tax on their gains, reaching zero by 2017; owners of stocks and tangible property held more than three years would also shield the inflation portion of their gains from tax. Because most capital gains are realized by higher-income households, the largest dollar benefits would flow to them, and the benefit would be delivered through mutual funds, real estate investment trusts, partnerships, and other investment vehicles, which the bill expressly covers [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Caps the tax rate on net capital gains at 20% for 1997, then reduces it one percentage point each year until it reaches zero for 2017 and later years [S2][S3].

For assets held more than three years, substitutes an inflation-indexed basis (measured by the GDP deflator) for the original purchase price, so price increases that only match inflation would no longer be taxed as gain [S3].

Carries both benefits through to investors via mutual funds, real estate investment trusts, partnerships, S corporations, and common trust funds, including rules letting regulated investment companies and REITs pass indexing adjustments through to their shareholders [S3].
Applies the lower rate against the alternative minimum tax as well, so investors could not be pushed back up to the old rate through that parallel tax [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, and ultimately taxpayers generally. Because the rate on capital gains falls every year and reaches zero in 2017, the revenue the government now collects when people sell appreciated assets would shrink year after year and eventually disappear, leaving other taxes to cover the difference [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: By 2017 the bill would tax capital gains at zero, eliminating this revenue source entirely and forcing other taxes, spending cuts, or borrowing to fill the gap [S2][S3].

Capital gains from selling stocks and businesses are realized mostly by higher-income households, so the tax savings would be concentrated at the top while the revenue loss is spread across everyone who pays taxes.

The bill would repeal the existing 50% exclusion for gain on small business stock and would limit individuals' deductible capital losses to the amount of their capital gains, tightening rules some investors rely on [S3].

Indexing would add real compliance burden: taxpayers would have to track inflation adjustments per asset, treat improvements of $1,000 or more as separate assets, and apply special rules for funds, trusts, short sales, and related-party transfers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrowly distributed: a guaranteed slide to a zero percent rate on investment gains plus inflation protection for long-held assets, both worth the most to the households that own the most stock and property. The cost is broad: a revenue source that phases down to nothing, plus added complexity and the loss of the small business stock break. An honest supporter would have to concede that the phase-out schedule was designed to make the eventual zero rate look gradual while locking it in permanently.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and sat there until the Congress ended, never getting a hearing, a vote, or even a cosponsor.

narrative.text: Rep. John Cooksey introduced the bill on May 1, 1997, as a standalone measure to cut the capital gains rate and index asset basis for inflation [S1][S3].
The House referred it to the Committee on Ways and Means the same day, and the action history shows no further steps — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor action [S5].
The bill attracted zero cosponsors over the life of the 105th Congress [S4].
The 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, and the bill expired in committee [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal Treasury kept the capital gains revenue this bill would have phased out to zero, and investors who would have benefited got nothing. No member paid any political price for letting it die.

for.name: Rep. John Cooksey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its only supporter of record; no colleague signed on as a cosponsor.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — letting it expire at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken on the bill; its sponsor was a Republican, and it drew no cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: The bill lets regulated investment companies pass inflation-indexing adjustments through to shareholders and drops the tax rate on gains toward zero, making fund investing more attractive and after-tax returns higher. The cost — shrinking capital gains revenue — falls on the Treasury, not the industry.

Tangible property is an indexed asset under the bill, and REIT shareholders receive the indexing adjustment in proportion to the trust's indexed holdings, sheltering the inflation portion of property gains from tax. The revenue loss is borne by all taxpayers.

industries.industry: Small business owners and their investors
industries.note: The bill repeals the existing 50% exclusion for gain on qualifying small business stock, removing a targeted break, while the falling general capital gains rate partially replaces it. Some small-business investors would come out ahead, others worse off depending on their situation.
